# Spiral bacteria

> *A painless genital ulcer that heals on its own can be the first sign of an infection that damages
> the aorta decades later, and a week of fever after wading through flood water can end in kidney
> failure. Both are caused by spirochaetes, thin coiled bacteria that bore through tissue and are hard
> to see or grow, and where each one lives decides how it reaches people.*

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Learning objectives
- Explain how flagella that lie inside the envelope let spirochaetes bore through tissue, and why
  spirochaetes are seldom seen on a Gram stain or grown in routine culture.
- Sort the spiral bacteria by shape and reservoir, and predict from the reservoir how each reaches
  people and whether it passes from person to person.
- Describe the stages of syphilis caused by *Treponema pallidum*, and explain why an infection without
  symptoms can still harm a fetus.
- Explain how *Leptospira* passes from rats to people through water and soil, and why leptospirosis
  follows floods.
- Name the host, setting and route that let each main organism cause disease.
- Tell *T. pallidum* from *Leptospira* by reservoir, route and time course.
:::

## The group {#sec-spir-group}

### The group in one sentence {#sec-spir-sentence}

**Spirochaetes** are long, thin, coiled bacteria whose flagella lie inside the envelope; they bore
through tissue, most are too thin to see on a Gram stain, and they are hard or impossible to grow, so
their infections are usually detected through the patient's antibodies or the bacteria's nucleic
acid. Most of the six questions have one answer for the whole group; its members differ mainly in
where they live, which decides how each reaches people.

| Question | Answer for the spirochaetes |
|---|---|
| What is it built from? | A long, thin, coiled cell with an envelope of the Gram-negative type: a thin peptidoglycan layer under an outer membrane. Its flagella are anchored near each end of the cell and lie beneath the outer membrane. In *T. pallidum* the outer membrane has no LPS, the endotoxin of other Gram-negative bacteria, and very few exposed proteins, so antibodies have little to bind, which helps it persist for years |
| How does it get energy, and what does it need to grow? | Its own metabolism, but *T. pallidum* has lost the genes for making many nutrients and takes them from the host, so it cannot be grown on ordinary laboratory media; *Leptospira* grows only slowly, over weeks, in special media |
| How does it copy itself and change? | Binary fission, slowly; *T. pallidum* remains susceptible to penicillin, but a single mutation in its ribosomal RNA, now common, makes it resistant to macrolides, drugs that act on the bacterial ribosome; *Borrelia* changes its surface proteins during an infection |
| Where does it live, and how does it spread? | *T. pallidum* in humans only, passed by sexual contact and across the placenta; *Leptospira* in the kidneys of rats and other animals, shed in their urine into water and soil; *Borrelia* carried to people by ticks or body lice |
| How does damage happen? | No single toxin explains the disease: the bacteria spread through tissue and in the blood, and much of the damage comes from the inflammation they provoke, particularly in and around small blood vessels |
| What does it have that my cells lack? | A peptidoglycan wall and bacterial ribosomes, the targets of antibacterial drugs |

In most bacteria that swim, the flagella project from the surface and turn like propellers (see [*How
bacteria are built and get energy*](bacteria-build-energy.qmd#sec-bact-extras)). In a spirochaete they
stay inside the envelope. When they rotate, the whole coiled cell turns and flexes like a corkscrew,
and this motion carries it through viscous material, such as mucus and the gel between cells, in which
bacteria with external flagella make little progress. Spirochaetes therefore cross mucosa, move
through tissue and reach the blood early in an infection.

*T. pallidum* and *Leptospira* are about 0.1 to 0.2 µm across, at the limit of resolution of the light
microscope (see [*The microbial world*](../foundations/microbial-world.qmd#sec-world-scale)), so they
cannot be seen after a Gram stain (see [*Detecting bacteria and testing
susceptibility*](detecting-bacteria.qmd#sec-dbac-microscopy)). **Dark-field microscopy**, in which the
specimen is lit from the side so that thin organisms shine against a dark background, shows them moving
in fluid from a genital or skin lesion; it is not used for lesions in the mouth, where harmless
treponemes that look the same live. *T. pallidum* cannot be grown on ordinary laboratory media, and
diagnostic laboratories do not culture it, because it depends on its host for nutrients it can no
longer make (see [*A map of the bacteria*](bacteria-map.qmd#sec-map-habitat)); in research
laboratories it grows only alongside living mammalian cells. Laboratories therefore detect most
spirochaetal infections by **serology**, detection of a patient's antibodies as evidence of exposure
(see [*Detecting and controlling microbes*](../foundations/detection-control.qmd#sec-det-serology)),
and by **nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs)**, tests that copy a target sequence many times until
it can be detected (see [*Detecting and controlling
microbes*](../foundations/detection-control.qmd#sec-det-molecular)).

*Campylobacter* and *Helicobacter pylori* are curved or spiral too, and they are grouped with the
spirochaetes because the group is named for a single trait, shape (see [*A map of the
bacteria*](bacteria-map.qmd#sec-map-names)). In other respects they are ordinary Gram-negative rods:
short, with flagella outside the cell, visible on a Gram stain, and grown on agar in an atmosphere
with little oxygen. Both are **microaerophiles**, which need oxygen but are damaged at normal
atmospheric levels (see [*How bacteria are built and get energy*](bacteria-build-energy.qmd#sec-bact-oxygen)).

### Sorting the group {#sec-spir-key}

We sort the spiral bacteria first by shape, which separates the spirochaetes from the curved gut
bacteria, and then by **reservoir**, where an organism normally lives and multiplies, because the
reservoir predicts how each one reaches people. *Borrelia* reaches people through a **vector**, an
arthropod that carries an organism between hosts.

::: {.concept-tree}
[Sorting the spiral bacteria by shape and reservoir]{.tree-title}

- Spirochaetes: long, thin and coiled, with flagella inside the envelope
  - Reservoir in humans only: *T. pallidum*
  - Reservoir in the kidneys of rats and other animals: *Leptospira*
  - Reservoir in animals, carried to people by ticks: *Borrelia*
- Curved Gram-negative rods, with flagella outside the cell
  - Reservoir in the gut of poultry and other animals: *Campylobacter*
  - Reservoir in the human stomach: *H. pylori*
:::

The reservoir predicts how the bacterium reaches people and what follows:

| Reservoir | How it reaches people | What follows |
|---|---|---|
| Humans only | Sexual contact with an infectious lesion; across the placenta | It passes from person to person, often from people who do not know they are infected, so screening and treating people breaks the chain |
| The kidneys of rats and other animals, which shed it in their urine | Water and soil contaminated with urine, through cuts, softened skin or mucosa | Illness follows floods and work or recreation in water and wet soil; people rarely pass it to one another |
| Animals, with ticks as the vector (for most species of *Borrelia*) | The bite of an infected tick | Disease occurs only where its ticks live |
| The gut of poultry and other animals | Swallowed in undercooked poultry, or in contaminated food or water | **Gastroenteritis**, inflammation of the stomach and intestines that causes vomiting, diarrhoea or both, prevented by thorough cooking and kitchen hygiene |
| The human stomach | From person to person, usually in childhood | Infection that lasts for decades unless treated |

Work through the key from the shape of the cell, and read at each branch what the trait predicts about
the bacterium.

<div data-island="sorting-key" data-src="/diagrams/spir-key.yml"></div>

## Main organisms {#sec-spir-main}

### *Treponema pallidum*: syphilis, in stages over years {#sec-spir-treponema}

*T. pallidum* causes **syphilis**, an infection that passes through stages over years. It lives only
in humans and is killed quickly by drying, so it passes only from person to person: by direct sexual
contact with an infectious lesion, and vertically, across the placenta from a pregnant woman to her
fetus (see [*Transmission, outbreaks and One
Health*](../foundations/transmission-outbreaks.qmd#sec-trans-routes)). It enters through the mucosa of
the genital tract, anus or mouth, or through small breaks in the skin, and it spreads in the lymph and
the blood early, before any lesion appears.

Untreated, the infection passes through four stages. The third, the latent stage, is a **latent
infection**, persistence of an organism in a silent state with the possibility of reactivation (see
[*Microbes and their hosts*](../foundations/host-microbe.qmd#sec-host-courses)).

| Stage | When it begins | What happens | Passed on by sexual contact? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Primary | Usually about three weeks after infection | A **chancre**, a painless ulcer at the site where the bacteria entered, with enlarged lymph nodes nearby; it heals without treatment within a few weeks | Yes, from the chancre |
| Secondary | Weeks to a few months after the chancre | The bacteria, carried in the blood, multiply throughout the body: a widespread rash, often including the palms and soles, with fever, enlarged lymph nodes and moist sores in the mouth and genital tract; these settle without treatment | Yes, readily, from the moist sores |
| Latent | Once the secondary stage settles | No symptoms, and the infection is found only by antibody tests; early in this stage the features of the secondary stage can return | Only while those features return; a pregnant woman can still infect her fetus |
| Tertiary (late) | Years to decades later, in some untreated people | Chronic inflammation damages the aorta, the brain and spinal cord, and other organs | No |

A chancre in the vagina, the anus or the mouth is easily missed, and the latent stage causes no
symptoms at all, so many infections are found only by serology.

*T. pallidum* has no known toxins. Where it settles, it provokes chronic inflammation around small
blood vessels, which narrows them and damages the tissue they supply, so most of the damage comes from
the host's response (see [*Microbes and their hosts*](../foundations/host-microbe.qmd#sec-host-drf)).
In late syphilis, inflammation of the small vessels that supply the wall of the aorta weakens it, and
an **aneurysm**, a localised widening of an artery, forms where the aorta leaves the heart. The
bacteria can reach the brain and meninges at any stage. Early in the infection they can cause
**meningitis**, inflammation of the meninges, the membranes that cover the brain and spinal cord, or
inflammation of the eye or the inner ear; the slowly progressive damage to the brain and spinal cord
appears years later.

Bacteria in a pregnant woman's blood can cross the placenta at any stage of pregnancy, most readily in
the early stages of her infection. **Congenital infection**, infection passed from mother to fetus
before birth, can cause miscarriage or stillbirth, or an infant born with congenital syphilis. The
mother often has no symptoms, so pregnant women are screened by serology, and treatment during
pregnancy prevents congenital syphilis.

Syphilis is diagnosed mainly by serology, with two kinds of antibody test used together. One detects
antibodies against proteins of *T. pallidum*; it usually stays positive for life, even after
treatment, and so shows that the person has been infected at some time. The other detects antibodies
against a lipid that is not specific to the bacterium; their level rises with active infection and
falls after successful treatment, so this test is used to judge whether the infection is active and
whether treatment has worked, although it can be positive in other conditions and negative in late
syphilis. Both tests can still be negative when the chancre first appears, so a NAAT on a swab from
the ulcer is used to detect the bacterium itself. *T. pallidum* has remained susceptible to
penicillin. Treatment at any stage ends the infection but cannot undo damage already done, and it
leaves no lasting immunity, so a person can be infected again.

| Pattern of harm | Mechanism | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Ulcer at the site of entry | The bacteria multiply where they entered, and inflammation around them breaks down the surface | A firm, painless ulcer on the penis three weeks after sexual contact, which heals on its own |
| Spread through the body | The bacteria are carried in the blood and settle in the skin, mucosa and lymph nodes, where they provoke inflammation | A rash on the trunk, palms and soles, with fever, two months after an ulcer healed |
| Late damage to organs | Years of chronic inflammation around small blood vessels damage the tissue they supply | An aneurysm of the aorta where it leaves the heart, decades after an untreated infection |
| Congenital infection | Bacteria in the mother's blood cross the placenta and infect the fetus | A stillbirth after a mother's infection went undetected in pregnancy |

::: {.callout-important}
## Is syphilis over when the ulcer heals?
The chancre is painless and heals without treatment within a few weeks, so its disappearance is easily
taken as the end of the infection. By the time the chancre appears, however, *T. pallidum* has already
spread in the lymph and the blood. Weeks later the rash of the secondary stage appears, and after it
settles the bacteria persist through the latent stage, when antibody tests remain positive and a
pregnant woman can still infect her fetus. Without treatment, the infection continues.
:::

Three conditions let *T. pallidum* cause disease:

| | Condition | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| Who (host) | A sexually active person, including one treated for syphilis before; a fetus whose mother has untreated syphilis | Treatment leaves no lasting immunity, so a person can be infected again; bacteria in the mother's blood cross the placenta |
| Where (setting) | Sexual contact with a person in the primary or secondary stage, who often does not know of the infection; pregnancy | The bacterium lives only in humans and is killed quickly by drying, so it passes by direct contact with a lesion, or across the placenta |
| How (route) | Through the mucosa or small breaks in the skin, then in the lymph and the blood throughout the body | Corkscrew motion carries it through tissue, and it spreads before the chancre appears |

Step through the two routes *T. pallidum* takes: through the body over years, and across the
placenta.

### *Leptospira*: from rat urine, through water and soil {#sec-spir-leptospira}

*Leptospira* are thin, tightly coiled spirochaetes with hooked ends. They need oxygen, and they grow
only slowly in special media. The species that cause disease live in the kidneys of rats, which carry
them without becoming ill, and of many other mammals, including dogs, pigs and cattle, which can
themselves become ill. All of these animals shed the bacteria in their urine for long periods.
Outside the host the bacteria survive for weeks or months in fresh water and moist soil, especially in
warm climates. **Leptospirosis**, infection with *Leptospira*, is therefore a
**zoonosis**, an infection transmitted from animals to humans (see [*Transmission, outbreaks and One
Health*](../foundations/transmission-outbreaks.qmd#sec-trans-chain)).

People meet the bacteria in water and soil that infected animals have contaminated. The bacteria enter
through cuts and abrasions, through skin softened by long immersion, or through the mucosa of the eye,
nose and mouth, including when contaminated water is swallowed. Exposure follows heavy rain and
flooding, and it comes with work and recreation in water and wet soil:

- Clearing drains
- Farming in wet fields
- Swimming and other sports in fresh water

Leptospirosis is acquired in Singapore and is common across South-East Asia. People rarely pass the
infection to one another, so each case comes from the contaminated environment.

::: {.example}
In 2000, many of the athletes who took part in an international multi-sport race in Sabah, Malaysian
Borneo, developed leptospirosis, and swimming in a river during the race was the main risk.
:::

The corkscrew motion of the bacteria carries them through tissue into the blood, which takes them to
every organ. The **incubation period**, the time between infection and the appearance of symptoms, is
usually one to two weeks, and illness then begins suddenly with fever, headache and muscle pain,
especially in the calves, and **conjunctival suffusion**, redness of the conjunctiva without pus or
discharge. Most infections are mild or cause no symptoms, and settle as antibodies clear the
bacteria from the blood. In a minority, the bacteria damage the lining of small blood vessels and the
organs they supply, and severe leptospirosis follows, with **jaundice**,
yellowing of the skin and the whites of the eyes as bilirubin accumulates in the blood, kidney
failure and bleeding. **Pulmonary
haemorrhage**, bleeding from damaged small vessels into the alveoli, is the most dangerous
complication.

In the first week of illness, while the bacteria are in the blood, a NAAT on a blood sample can detect
them. Antibodies appear from about the end of the first week, so serology confirms the infection
later, most clearly when the antibody level rises between an early sample and a later one. Treatment
is with antibacterial drugs, and severe disease also needs support for the failing organs.
Prevention follows the route:

- Covering cuts
- Wearing boots and gloves in water and wet soil
- Avoiding swimming in water that may be contaminated
- Controlling rats

| Pattern of harm | Mechanism | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Fever with muscle pain | The bacteria spread in the blood to every organ, and the host's response to them causes fever and muscle pain | Fever, headache, calf pain and red eyes a week after wading through flood water |
| Jaundice and kidney failure | The bacteria damage the lining of small blood vessels and the cells of the liver and kidney | A farm worker with yellow skin and a rising blood creatinine in the second week of illness |
| Pulmonary haemorrhage | Damaged small vessels in the lungs leak blood into the alveoli | Coughing up blood and difficulty breathing, with a high risk of death |

Three conditions let *Leptospira* cause disease:

| | Condition | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| Who (host) | Anyone exposed to contaminated water or soil, especially with cuts or abrasions or after long immersion; healthy people are infected | The bacteria cross small breaks in the skin and the mucosa, and no failure of host defence is needed |
| Where (setting) | Fresh water and wet soil contaminated with the urine of rats and other animals, especially after heavy rain and floods; work in drains and wet fields, and sport in fresh water | Infected animals shed the bacteria in their urine for long periods, and the bacteria survive for weeks in warm, wet surroundings |
| How (route) | Through cuts, softened skin or the mucosa of the eye, nose and mouth, then in the blood to every organ | Corkscrew motion carries the bacteria through tissue and into the blood |

Step through the route *Leptospira* takes, from rat urine to the kidney and the lungs.

## Contrast pair {#sec-spir-pairs}

### *T. pallidum* and *Leptospira* {#sec-spir-pair-treponema-leptospira}

*T. pallidum* and *Leptospira* are both spirochaetes, alike in shape and movement and in how hard they
are to see and grow. Compare them feature by feature before reading the principle.

## Beyond the main organisms {#sec-spir-beyond}

### Supporting organisms {#sec-spir-supporting}

| Organism | Where it lives | What separates it | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|---|
| *Borrelia* | Ticks, which pick it up from small mammals; for one species, body lice, which pass it between people | A spirochaete carried to people by ticks or lice; during an infection it can change its surface proteins | Some species cause **Lyme disease**, an infection carried by ticks that begins with an expanding red rash around the bite and can later inflame the joints, nerves or heart; it occurs in temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere, such as North America and Europe, and is not acquired in Singapore. Other species cause **relapsing fever**, episodes of fever that return as the bacteria change their surface proteins and escape the antibodies made against the previous variant |
| *Campylobacter* | The gut of poultry and other animals | A curved Gram-negative rod with flagella outside the cell; a microaerophile | One of the most common causes of bacterial gastroenteritis: diarrhoea, often with blood, abdominal pain and fever after eating undercooked poultry. In a small minority it is followed weeks later by **Guillain–Barré syndrome**, a paralysis that develops over days to weeks as the immune response damages the peripheral nerves; antibodies against the bacterium's surface cross-react with the nerves, an example of **molecular mimicry**, host damage caused by antibodies or T cells raised against a microbe cross-reacting with host tissue (see [*How bacteria cause damage*](bacterial-damage.qmd#sec-bdam-host)) |
| *H. pylori* | The mucus layer over the lining of the human stomach; usually acquired in childhood and carried for decades | A curved Gram-negative rod that swims into the mucus with its flagella; its **urease**, an enzyme that splits urea into ammonia and carbon dioxide, makes ammonia that neutralises acid around it | Causes **gastritis**, inflammation of the stomach lining, in nearly everyone it infects, usually without symptoms; some infected people develop **peptic ulcers**, breaches in the lining of the stomach or duodenum, and a few develop gastric cancer. Clearing the infection lets ulcers heal and stops most of them returning (see the practice case in [*The microbial world*](../foundations/microbial-world.qmd#sec-world-case)) |

### Later in the course {#sec-spir-later}

| Organism | Where it comes up again |
|---|---|
| *T. pallidum* | Sexual health (the stages of syphilis); obstetrics and neonatology (screening in pregnancy and congenital syphilis); cardiology and neurology (late syphilis) |
| *Leptospira* | Infectious diseases (fever after exposure to water or soil); renal and respiratory medicine (kidney failure and pulmonary haemorrhage in severe leptospirosis) |
| *Borrelia* | Travel medicine (Lyme disease and relapsing fever) |
| *Campylobacter* | Gastroenterology (bacterial gastroenteritis); neurology (Guillain–Barré syndrome) |
| *H. pylori* | Gastroenterology (gastritis and peptic ulcers); oncology (gastric cancer) |
